title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (and enumerated bullet markers like '2.', '3.', '4. **') that begin items in a numbered list, regardless of the list's topic. It activates most strongly on bare list-number tokens themselves, and more weakly on other sentences that happen to co-occur in a numbered-list context (e.g., advice or pros/cons lists) such as the AITA-style relationship advice seen in the random examples. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking any list-numbering structure, or on bulleted lists that use symbols rather than numerals, since the trigger is specifically the enumerator token marking sequence position rather than the content or sentiment of the text.

title: Affirming self-worth reassurance
description: This latent fires on direct second-person affirmations that validate the listener's inherent worth, strength, and entitlement to happiness, love, respect, and self-care (e.g., 'You are strong, capable, and deserving of love and respect', 'Remember, you deserve to be happy and fulfilled'). It activates most strongly on formulaic therapeutic/self-help phrasing built around 'You are...' or 'Remember, you deserve/are...' templates emphasizing worthiness, capability, and prioritizing one's own well-being. It does not activate on general advice-giving, questions, boundary-setting suggestions, or empathetic reflections about the situation that lack this direct affirming '(You) are/deserve worthy' structure -- e.g., sentences offering practical steps, asking clarifying questions, or discussing other people's perspectives score low even if emotionally supportive in tone.

title: Actionable advice list item
description: This latent fires on bolded or emphasized imperative-style list items that give a concrete, practical tip, typically within a listicle of money-saving or lifestyle advice. It activates on short directive phrases (often starting with a bolded action verb or noun phrase followed by a colon) that instruct the reader to perform a specific task, such as 'Cook your own meals: Prepare simple, affordable meals using your groceries.' It would not activate on narrative prose, general discussion, or explanatory sentences that lack the imperative/bolded-tip list format, even if they cover similar frugality or self-care topics. The key trigger is the structural pattern of a highlighted action item followed by a brief elaboration, rather than the topic of cooking or budgeting itself.

title: List-item and step marker onset
description: This latent fires on the tokens that begin an enumerated list item or numbered step (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.') and on short introductory words like 'By' or 'Consider' that begin a gerund-led method clause (e.g., 'By communicating...', 'By having an...') within advice-style structured text. It activates most strongly on the bare numeral-plus-period token itself and on the initial word of a sentence that frames a method or suggestion, capturing the structural/formatting role of marking a discrete item or step rather than any topical content. It does not activate strongly on full declarative advice sentences that lack this list/step-initial marker or gerund-fronted 'By ___' construction, even when they express similar advice content, nor on numbers appearing mid-sentence or in non-list contexts.

title: Compound scheduling question
description: This latent fires on requests that ask another person to specify two related pieces of time/scheduling information in a single question, typically phrased as a polite request ('Could you tell me...') followed by two linked sub-questions joined by 'and'. It activates on sentences seeking coordination details—such as when someone will be available and when a corresponding event or deadline occurs—reflecting logistical planning between two parties. It would not activate on simple single-fact questions, statements providing schedule information rather than requesting it, or unrelated polite requests that don't involve coordinating timing between two linked events.

title: Casual positive-experience recap
description: This latent fires on short, informal first-person statements recounting a pleasant past experience or event, often using simple past tense and everyday vocabulary (e.g., 'had a great time,' 'yesterday'). It activates on sentences that express personal enjoyment or satisfaction retrospectively, typically in a conversational, small-talk register. It would not activate on formal, technical, or third-person descriptions, nor on statements expressing negative emotions, future plans, or abstract opinions unrelated to a concrete personal experience.

title: Formulaic advice-response preamble
description: This latent fires on stock introductory phrases that an AI advice-giver uses to frame a response before delivering substantive content: exclamations acknowledging a situation's difficulty ('dilemma!', 'What a tricky situation!', 'Oh boy, this is a tough one!') and meta-statements signaling the stance of the upcoming answer ('I'm going to give you a nuanced answer', 'I'll try to provide a balanced perspective', 'I'm here to help you navigate this situation'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic, often exclamatory openers that name or characterize the problem/tone rather than engage with its content. It does not activate (or activates weakly) on the actual substantive advice, empathetic elaboration, specific suggestions, or content-rich sentences that follow these preambles, even when those sentences discuss similar situations, since the latent tracks the rhetorical framing move itself rather than the topic or advice content.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an enumerated list item (e.g., '2', '3.', '4.', '9', often followed by bold text or a colon), rather than on the semantic content of the item itself. It activates most strongly on bare digit tokens marking list position, and also fires more weakly on fuller list-item sentences that still begin with a number/bullet plus a bolded lead phrase. It would not activate on prose sentences lacking a leading enumerator, even if they express similar advice-giving or step-by-step content, since the trigger is the structural list-numbering token rather than the topic or advice being given.
